Hood Heroes - épisode 6 : Ernest Edmond: Hood Heroes - Episode 6: Ernest Edmond, or How Sports Foster Youth Engagement
Jeune joueur de basket-ball plein d’ambi: A young basketball player full of ambition, he one day runs into unexpected obstacles on his path to his dream.
Ernest Edmond, le fondateur des Ballons: Ernest Edmond, founder of Les Ballons Intensifs Photo: Melissa Haouari
Le samedi matin dans un certain coin de: On Saturday mornings in a certain corner of Pointe-aux-Trembles, you can hear the sound of kids running in one of the neighbourhood’s gyms. It’s basketball training led by the team from the non-profit organization Les Ballons Intensifs (LBI), which offers a basketball training camp to youth in different Montréal neighbourhoods. What makes this service special? It’s completely free.
L’instigateur de ce projet est Ernest Ed: The driving force behind the project is Ernest Edmond. Arriving from Haiti at the age of six, the coach and founder of LBI has lived his whole life in the east end of Montréal, specifically in Pointe-aux-Trembles. A young basketball player full of ambition, he one day ran into unexpected obstacles on his path to his dream. In the hope of building ties between youth and the community, he sees sport as a brilliant way to get involved and give back to young people, while getting them actively involved in society.
Tout débute en 2008. Âgé d’à peine 18 an: It all began in 2008. Barely 18 years old, Ernest was preparing to leave for Florida, hoping to join a university basketball team. “During the tryout tests, I was diagnosed with a heart arrhythmia,” he says thoughtfully. “So I couldn’t keep training to make it onto a team.” Back in Quebec, the young athlete received more bad news. “I was told my cousin had died when I got back from the United States,” he explains. “Like me, he came from an immigrant family and grew up in the east end of Montréal, but he got involved in criminal activity that led to his death…” The death of his cousin, whom he was very close to, shook Ernest. “That year was supposed to be a springboard for me. In the end, it was the opposite.”
L’été suivant, Ernest s’est rapproché de: The following summer, Ernest grew closer to his cousin, who had lost his brother some time before. “Jimmy was 16 and wanted to make a youth basketball team in the fall. He asked me to train him over the summer,” he continues. “So every day that summer, we went to the park at 6 a.m. We trained for three or four hours, and then I went to work. After two weeks, Jimmy’s friends, who he spent the rest of his days with, noticed he was improving,” he says, referring to his cousin’s progress in basketball. “One of Jimmy’s friends joined us; he wanted to train with us and see progress. It went on like that until the end of the summer.” That year was only the beginning: thanks to word of mouth, several young people joined Ernest and Jimmy. “I put my time into those training sessions because I saw myself in those kids.”
« J’ai remarqué que les jeunes aimaient: “I noticed the kids liked it; a lot of them came,” he says. He explains that after some time, he found himself with about twenty young people under his wing. “I was struck by how popular the basketball training was with the kids. They were there every day at 6 a.m. sharp. They wanted to work hard,” he recalls. “They had needs to be met, requests tied to what they were going through, because not all of them could join teams you have to pay for.” Determined to respond to young people’s need for access to sport, Ernest continues: “At the end of the summer of 2013, I sat down with them. I asked them, ‘What do you concretely want?’” The answers all came back to the same request: they wanted Ernest to keep offering quality training, and to do it for free.
Quelques années plus tard, le désir des: A few years later, the young people’s wish came true, and it continues to grow. Ernest played a crucial role in answering the community’s demand: in 2013, he founded Les Ballons Intensifs, a free summer camp offering quality basketball training to anyone willing to put in the effort. Drawing on his personal experience, Ernest gives his time to young people and commits himself to them. “In a way, through the time I dedicate to them, I see it as the reward for their motivation and their efforts.”
<strong>Le basket-ball comme modèle d’en: Basketball as a model of civic engagement
Ses années d’expérience en tant qu’entra: His years of experience coaching young people in the neighbourhoods have helped Ernest better understand what the new generations are going through. “I grew up in the east end of Montréal, in a neighbourhood that’s a bit forgotten and neglected, but I had a different path. I played basketball, but I also did theatre. I was very involved in my school council and I was in an enriched program. Other kids had more atypical, more difficult paths, I’m aware of that,” he says. That is nonetheless one of the reasons he wants to make quality sport accessible to as many young people as possible, no matter what they’re going through.
Avec le temps, ceux qu’il prend sous son: Over time, more and more young people came under his wing. “Little by little, the kids shared their concerns, their problems with me. Notions of civic participation developed, in the sense that they were asking questions: ‘Why don’t our basketball nets ever get replaced? Why don’t we have a working water fountain in our parks?’” he says. The more his students progressed in sport, the more they became aware of the problems around them. “The kids notice concerns. Before, they didn’t have the chance to get actively involved in the community; most of them came from different, disadvantaged backgrounds. There were language barriers, financial barriers that kept them from participating,” he continues. For the coach, the lack of opportunities for engagement is a problem. It is therefore essential to create ways for young people to get involved.
« On va devenir un modèle d’engagement,: “We’re going to become a model of engagement, and we’re going to make a shift so that it turns into youth engagement. We’re going to use sport to get young people more engaged in their community.” Those were Ernest’s words in 2013, when he wanted to encourage the young people in his neighbourhood to give of themselves for their community. For him, that wish is even more relevant today, in a context where young people are more disconnected than ever from certain issues and where there are unique problems in some of the more disadvantaged neighbourhoods.
Lorsqu’on le questionne sur l’implicatio: Asked about youth involvement, the coach from Pointe-aux-Trembles says he wants to foster young people’s engagement in a variety of ways. Drawing on his experience, he sees engagement at different levels. “My team and I wanted to break down our approach. To approach engagement in several stages, the way we do with sport,” explains the founder of Les Ballons Intensifs. He adds that, modelled on sport, engagement can happen on both a personal and a professional level, and that through basketball, “young people can help restore the image of the sport and of the environment they play it in.”
« L’une des principales demandes des jeu: “One of the main requests from young people is to have free activities, because not all their parents can pay for them,” says Ernest. Having himself come from a neglected neighbourhood and faced personal challenges, the coach explains that free programming is a key element of access to sport for young people, especially in disadvantaged neighbourhoods.
Et s’il insiste sur la question de la gr: And while he insists on free programming, that doesn’t mean the quality of the service offered should be any lower. For Ernest, “free and accessible shouldn’t mean cheap and poor quality.” He is firm: “I don’t want people to associate free youth involvement with a disadvantaged neighbourhood. When I look for funding, for example, I count on the fact that donors aren’t funding a problem, but a solution.”
« Il y a des parents qui veulent nous pa: “There are parents who want to pay us for the service we offer their kids, but I always refuse. I don’t want basketball to cost money, and I don’t want there to be classes of kids. On the court, everyone is on the same level,” Ernest continues. “We ask for nothing; only the young people’s involvement and effort,” adds the coach. While some parents are willing to pay so their children can access extracurricular sports activities, others simply can’t. Faced with these different realities, Ernest explains: “Some parents don’t speak the language, others work several jobs at once – all of that makes access difficult. For me, Les Ballons Intensifs is a way to give every young person the same chance.”
<strong>Changer la perception des jeunes: Changing perceptions of young people and of basketball
Le basket-ball a souvent une image négat: Basketball often has a negative image. For Ernest, “there has always been a negative culture associated with the sport.” What motivated him to get involved in engaged sport was his desire to break down the negative stereotypes tied to basketball.
Ernest raconte que, malgré l’évolution d: Ernest says that, despite the evolution in how sport is perceived in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, the positive effects of sports activities on the community still aren’t given their due. “When I was younger, we hung out a lot in one particular park to play basketball,” he recalls. “We called it the ‘dragon park’ in Pointe-aux-Trembles. It was surrounded by houses, and one day the City decided to close it because residents were complaining about the noise. It was the only place around where we could play basketball. We found it a bit insulting because it wasn’t happening to sports fields in other neighbourhoods. So now, we’re trying to meet young people’s need for access to basketball courts pretty much everywhere in the neighbourhoods.”
« Quand on parle d’engagement jeunesse,: “When we talk about youth engagement, it’s important to talk about positive influence in the community,” says Ernest, picking up momentum. “I don’t want people to see kids who take part in community activities as problem kids, but as kids who are worth it.”
Impliqué dans sa communauté depuis des a: Involved in his community for years, the coach seeks to give back to those who make an effort and who commit. “There are plenty of ways to measure young people’s impact in their neighbourhood,” says Ernest. “My ideal is that, in the communities where we work, young people take ownership of the project. There’s nothing more beautiful than that moment when a young person asks to get involved, asks to expand the project in their neighbourhood,” he says, stars in his eyes.
Selon Ernest, il y a une réalité qu’on o: According to Ernest, there is a reality that often gets forgotten when we talk about civic engagement. “I’d like us to rethink engagement in the neighbourhoods too, because it’s a pretty elitist concept. Not everyone can get involved. When you come from a certain background or live in financial precarity, it’s not easy to volunteer in community life,” he explains. He draws attention to the accessibility of engagement, a concept everyone should be working on. “Getting involved somewhere takes more than time. It’s more demanding, it involves sacrifices. It has to be easier for young people to participate,” he adds. On a more optimistic note, he acknowledges that young people’s engagement in the neighbourhoods through sport has grown markedly stronger. “Every year, the number of young people who want to sign up with us goes up. We started with 20 kids in a single borough. Today, we have more than 300 young people in 4 boroughs of the city,” says the resident happily. “My dream is to see more and more young people solving their community’s problems by being creative, by showing leadership,” confides Ernest.
« On pense que les jeunes des quartiers: “We believe young people in the neighbourhoods are part of the solutions, because they live it every day, they understand it,” he concludes. For him, community involvement remains essential, but he nonetheless stresses the importance of action. “Young people need to have expectations. Of others and of themselves. When they have high expectations, it pushes them to act and to change things,” he explains. “Training my cousin was a tiny favour. But if I hadn’t acted at that moment, none of this would have been possible.”
